transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: Transportation officials in London have launched a new smartphone application designed to make commuting easier and more efficient for the city's millions of daily travelers. The app, called London Journey Planner, integrates real-time data from all of the city's transportation networks—including the Underground, buses, trains, river buses, and even the city's bicycle share program—allowing users to plan door-to-door routes and receive live updates about delays, service changes, and platform alterations. One innovative feature is the app's ability to suggest less crowded carriages during peak travel times, using data from weight sensors installed in trains. The app also includes information about step-free access for passengers with mobility challenges, as well as real-time availability of docking stations for the bicycle share program. Since its launch last month, the app has been downloaded over 500,000 times, with early users reporting that it has reduced their average commute times by approximately 10 percent. Transportation officials say they plan to add features for electric vehicle charging stations and carpooling matching in the coming months.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: A new national survey conducted by the Youth Sports Alliance reveals that participation in organized sports among children aged 6 to 12 has declined by 12 percent over the past decade, raising concerns among health and education experts. The survey, which included responses from over 10,000 families across the United States, found that the average child now spends less than three hours per week playing organized sports, compared to nearly four and a half hours ten years ago. Researchers point to several factors contributing to this decline, including the rising cost of participation fees and equipment, increasing pressure on children to focus on academic achievement, and the growing popularity of screen-based entertainment like video games and social media. Perhaps most concerning, the survey found that children from low-income families are three times less likely to participate in organized sports than their wealthier peers, due to cost barriers and lack of access to facilities in underserved neighborhoods. Health experts warn that reduced physical activity in childhood is linked to higher rates of obesity, diabetes, and mental health problems later in life. In response to these findings, the Youth Sports Alliance is calling on schools and community organizations to expand free or low-cost sports programs and to reduce the emphasis on competitive specialization, which they say discourages many children from continuing to play sports for fun.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Female)
paras: Scientists at a Finnish research institute have developed a new type of packaging material made entirely from agricultural waste that could significantly reduce plastic pollution from food packaging. The innovative material, which is created using wheat straw and other plant fibers left over from farming, is fully biodegradable, breaking down completely in soil within just three months, compared to conventional plastic packaging which can take hundreds of years to decompose. Unlike previous bioplastics, which often require industrial composting facilities to break down properly, this new material decomposes naturally in home compost piles and even in marine environments. The researchers say the material is just as strong and water-resistant as traditional plastic packaging, making it suitable for a wide range of food products including fresh produce, dry goods, and even frozen foods. Several major food companies have already expressed interest in adopting the new packaging, with the first products featuring the material expected to appear on supermarket shelves within the next two years. The research team estimates that widespread adoption of this and similar materials could reduce plastic packaging waste by up to 70 percent in the food industry.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Ryan): Hey, Chloe. Did you see the email about summer internships? The deadline for applications is next Friday, and I still haven't decided which ones to apply for. How many are you planning to apply to?

Woman (Chloe): I'm going to apply to about four or five, I think. I don't want to put all my eggs in one basket, but I also don't want to spread myself too thin writing dozens of applications. Have you been to any of the information sessions yet?

Man: I went to the one for the marketing internships at the big consumer goods company downtown. It sounds really interesting—they have rotations in different departments, and they pay pretty well, like $20 an hour. But I've heard they're extremely competitive—they only take 15 interns from across the country.

Woman: That is competitive. What about the internship program at the local startup incubator? I went to their information session yesterday. They place interns with small tech companies around the city. The pay isn't as high—only $15 an hour—but they offer a lot more hands-on experience because the companies are small. You wouldn't just be getting coffee and making copies; you'd be actually working on real projects that matter to the business.

Man: That does sound valuable. But I'm also considering applying for an internship at the advertising agency where my cousin works. She said she could refer me, which would definitely help my chances. The problem is that it's unpaid. My parents are helping with tuition, but I still need to make money over the summer to cover my rent and living expenses next semester.

Woman: Unpaid internships are really tough. I think it's important to get good experience, but you can't work for free if you need to pay bills. Have you looked at the internships offered through the university's career services? They have partnerships with a lot of companies that specifically want to hire students from our school, and I think they're all paid positions. There's one with the university's marketing department that sounds right up your alley—they're looking for someone to help with social media and event promotion.

Man: Oh, I didn't know about that. Working on campus would be convenient too. I wouldn't have to commute downtown every day, which would save money on transportation. What kind of internships are you applying for? You're a graphic design major, right?

Woman: Yeah, I'm looking at design internships mostly. I found one at a book publishing company that sounds perfect—they need someone to help design book covers and marketing materials. I'm also applying for a position at a small design studio that does a lot of non-profit work. The pay isn't amazing, but their portfolio is really impressive, and I think I'd learn a lot there.

Man: That sounds great. Hey, would you want to meet up this weekend to work on our applications and resumes together? Sometimes it helps to have another person look over your materials and give feedback. I always find it hard to talk about my own strengths.

Woman: That's a great idea. We can meet at the library on Sunday afternoon. I'll bring my laptop and we can take turns reviewing each other's cover letters. I definitely struggle with those too—it feels like I'm just repeating the same thing over and over.

Man: Perfect. And we should both make sure to get our applications in before the deadline, even if that means submitting them a day or two early. The career center said that many companies review applications on a rolling basis, so applying early can give you an advantage.
Woman: Good point. I'll see you Sunday then. Good luck with your applications!

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Jack): Hey, Lily. That's a nice camera you have there. Are you into photography? I've been thinking about getting a camera myself, but I don't really know where to start.

Woman (Lily): Thanks, Jack! Yeah, photography has been my hobby for about three years now. I absolutely love it. What made you interested in getting a camera? Do you just want to take better photos for your social media, or are you looking to get more serious about it?

Man: I'm not sure yet. I've always enjoyed taking photos when I travel, but my phone camera just doesn't capture things the way I see them, especially in low light or when I want to get those nice blurry backgrounds in portraits. But I'm also worried that if I buy an expensive camera, I'll end up not using it much, like that guitar I bought last year that's just sitting in my closet.

Woman: That's a valid concern. Photography can be an expensive hobby if you get really into it. My advice would be not to buy the most expensive camera right away. You can get a really good entry-level DSLR or mirrorless camera for around $500 to $600, and you can always upgrade later if you stick with it. Actually, you could even look into buying a used camera body from a reputable seller—cameras hold their value really well, and you can save a lot of money that way.
Man: What about lenses? I've heard that lenses are actually more important than the camera body. Do I need to buy a bunch of different lenses right away?

Woman: No, definitely not. The kit lens that comes with most entry-level cameras is actually pretty versatile for general use—it can zoom from wide angle for landscapes to moderate telephoto for portraits. After you've been shooting for a while and you know what kinds of photography you enjoy most, then you can think about buying additional lenses. For example, if you love taking portraits, you might want a prime lens with a wide aperture for that blurry background effect you mentioned. If you're into wildlife or sports, you'd need a telephoto zoom lens. But there's no need to buy all that at the beginning.
Man: That makes sense. What do you like to photograph the most?

Woman: I really love street photography—just walking around the city and capturing candid moments of people going about their daily lives. There's something special about capturing a moment that will never happen again exactly the same way. I also do a lot of landscape photography when I go hiking on weekends. It gets me outside and helps me appreciate nature more. What kind of photos do you think you'd enjoy taking?

Man: I think I'd like landscape and travel photography mostly. I go hiking and camping pretty often with my friends, and it would be great to have better photos from those trips. Maybe I'd also like to try astrophotography—taking photos of the night sky and stars. That looks amazing when people do it well, but I hear it's pretty challenging.

Woman: Astrophotography is a lot of fun, but it does require some specific equipment and a lot of patience. You need a sturdy tripod, for one thing, and a lens that can open wide to let in a lot of light. But it's incredibly rewarding when you get a good shot of the Milky Way. If you end up getting a camera, we should go out shooting together sometime. I'm always happy to show people the basics and share tips.
Man: That would be awesome! I really appreciate the advice. Maybe I'll start by going to a camera store this weekend to look at some different models and see how they feel in my hands.

Woman: That's a great idea. Holding a camera and testing the controls is really important before you buy—some cameras feel better in your hands than others, depending on the size and button layout. And don't let the salespeople talk you into buying more than you need right away. Remember, start simple.
Man: I'll keep that in mind. Thanks so much for all the help, Lily!

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: Plastic pollution in the world's oceans has become one of the most pressing environmental issues of our time, with an estimated 8 million tons of plastic waste entering marine ecosystems every year. This plastic comes from a variety of sources, including single-use packaging, discarded fishing gear, and microbeads from personal care products. Once in the ocean, plastic never fully biodegrades—it simply breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, which can persist in the environment for centuries.

The impact of plastic pollution on marine life is devastating. Sea turtles, whales, seabirds, and fish often mistake plastic debris for food, leading to internal injuries, intestinal blockages, and starvation. It's estimated that over 90 percent of seabirds have plastic fragments in their stomachs, and nearly 700 marine species have been documented to be affected by plastic pollution either through ingestion or entanglement. Discarded fishing nets, often called "ghost gear," are particularly dangerous, as they continue to trap and kill marine animals for years after being lost or abandoned.

The problem also extends to human health, as microplastics have been found in seafood, drinking water, and even table salt. While research is still ongoing into the long-term health effects of consuming microplastics, scientists have raised concerns about the chemicals used in plastic production, many of which are known to be toxic or hormone-disrupting.

Addressing ocean plastic pollution requires action at multiple levels. Many countries have already implemented bans on single-use plastics like straws, cutlery, and shopping bags, and companies are under increasing pressure to develop more sustainable packaging alternatives and take responsibility for the entire lifecycle of their products. Beach clean-up efforts, while helpful for removing existing debris, cannot solve the problem alone—experts emphasize that reducing plastic production and improving waste management systems globally are essential for long-term solutions. Individuals can also make a difference by reducing their own plastic consumption, properly disposing of waste, and supporting policies that address the root causes of plastic pollution.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Music has been an integral part of human culture for thousands of years, but modern neuroscience research is revealing that learning to play a musical instrument can have profound and lasting effects on brain development and cognitive function. Unlike almost every other activity, playing music engages practically every part of the brain simultaneously, particularly the areas responsible for visual processing, auditory processing, and motor coordination.

One of the most well-documented benefits of musical training is improved executive function—the set of mental processes that includes working memory, problem-solving, attention control, and cognitive flexibility. Studies have consistently shown that children who receive at least two years of musical training perform better on tasks requiring these skills compared to children with no musical training. This is because reading music and playing an instrument requires constant monitoring and adjustment—musicians must process notes on a page, translate them into precise motor movements, listen carefully to the sound they're producing, and make real-time adjustments to maintain rhythm and pitch.

Musical training also appears to enhance language skills. Because music and language share many of the same neural pathways in the brain, musicians often show enhanced ability to distinguish between different speech sounds, which can be particularly beneficial for children learning to read or for people learning a second language. Research has also found that musicians have better auditory working memory, allowing them to hold and manipulate more information in their minds when listening.

Contrary to popular belief, it's never too late to benefit from musical training. While children's brains are more plastic and adaptable, studies have shown that older adults who take up a musical instrument experience improvements in memory, attention, and processing speed, even after just a few months of regular practice. Playing music can also be an effective way to reduce stress and anxiety, as it requires focused attention that can take people's minds off their worries, much like meditation.

However, researchers emphasize that these benefits come from active engagement with playing an instrument, not simply from listening to music. While listening to music can certainly be enjoyable and have mood-boosting effects, the significant cognitive benefits appear to come from the sustained effort and multisensory coordination involved in learning to play.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: More and more college students are choosing to start their own businesses while still in school, rather than waiting until after graduation. This trend reflects both changing economic realities and a growing entrepreneurial culture on many college campuses. Today's students have grown up with stories of successful young founders like Mark Zuckerberg, who started Facebook from his dorm room, and many see entrepreneurship as an attractive alternative to traditional employment.

There are several advantages to starting a business while still in college. For one thing, students have access to a wide range of resources that may be harder to come by after graduation, including entrepreneurship centers, business plan competitions with cash prizes, mentorship from business professors, and networks of alumni who are often willing to help young founders. Many colleges also offer seed funding programs for student startups, and some even provide free office space or legal services. Additionally, college is a relatively low-risk time to experiment with entrepreneurship—if a business fails, students don't have to worry about supporting a family or paying a mortgage, and they haven't yet given up a steady salary to pursue their idea.

Student entrepreneurs are launching businesses across a wide range of industries, from tech startups and apps to food businesses, creative services, and social enterprises. Some of the most successful student startups have been those that solve problems students themselves face on campus—everything from textbook rental services to laundry delivery apps to platforms for connecting students with part-time jobs.

However, starting a business while in school also presents significant challenges. Balancing the demands of running a company with academic coursework can be extremely stressful, and many student entrepreneurs struggle with time management and burnout. There's also the financial risk—even with seed funding, most startups require some initial investment, and the vast majority of new businesses fail within their first few years. Some critics argue that focusing too much on entrepreneurship can detract from the educational experience, causing students to neglect their studies.

Despite these challenges, many educators believe that the entrepreneurial skills students gain through starting a business—including problem-solving, resilience, creativity, and leadership—are incredibly valuable regardless of whether their company ultimately succeeds or fails. Whether or not they go on to run their own companies, these skills will serve them well in any career path they choose.
